lessons.title: Let’s count the real space locations first, and then talk about band representation
lessons.summary: Use orbit–stabilizer to distinguish site induction from full-k-star induction.

sections.title: One seed generates a complete orbit
sections.text: Apply every Seitz representative to seed r₀, then remove duplicates modulo full lattice translations. A general position in space group 2 generates r₀ and −r₀; an inversion center generates one site. These are real-space sites in a primitive cell, not arms of a momentum star.

sections.title: stabilizer To really fix the site
sections.text: If Rr₀+t differs from r₀ by an integer lattice vector L, replace the representative’s translation with t−L to obtain a site-stabilizer element that fixes r₀ exactly. Output lists both the subtracted L and the actual fixing translation.

sections.title: The local degree of freedom determines the fiber dimension
sections.text: Put an s orbital at each site for m-dimensional Bloch fiber; put a complete p triplet for 3m dimensions. p is reducible at some sites stabilizer , so it cannot be directly called an irreducible local representation, nor can it be automatically called EBR.

sections.title: Check between classroom and workbench
sections.text: First look at the site table and stabilizer table, and then observe the decomposition of Γ point character . The two-dimensional representation of group 2 general position s is divided into one part even parity and one part odd parity. Local D numbers are sorted with calculations and the inversion character is applied to identify them.

lessons.title: How to add phase to the sites crossing the primitive cell boundary
lessons.summary: Derive lattice-translation remainders, actions between fibers, and screw squares from periodic Bloch sums.

sections.title: Fix the gauge first
sections.text: Use the periodic gauge: Bloch coefficients include lattice vector T but omit orbital center rₐ from the exponential. Translation T_L therefore has eigenphase exp(−2πi k·L). Gauge changes alter matrix elements, so formulas from different gauges must not be mixed.

sections.title: Two parts of one operation
sections.text: After solving Rrₐ+t=r_b+L, the matrix block is the local s/p transformation multiplied by exp[−2πi(R⁻ᵀk)·L]. A general operation maps the k fiber to R⁻ᵀk. Only little-group operations preserving k modulo reciprocal-lattice vectors have physical characters within the same fiber.

sections.title: A screw operation squares to a translation
sections.text: This site’s space group 4 has its screw axis along z. Applying 2₁ twice gives a z-directed lattice translation, so its representation squares to −I at k_z=1/2 and has eigenvalues ±i. Omitting phases when sites cross cell boundaries incorrectly gives the square +I.
sections.formula: U_S(k)² = exp(−2πi k_z) I； λ_{±} = ±exp(−iπ k_z)

sections.title: View branch exchange along axis
sections.text: The second plot shows real and imaginary parts of complex eigenvalues, not band energies. The positive and negative labels exchange when k_z increases by one reciprocal period. Energy degeneracy, connectivity and insulating behavior additionally require a Hamiltonian and other constraints; this curve alone cannot establish them.

lessons.title: From matrices to characters and little-group decomposition
lessons.summary: Examining phase, dimensionality and irreducible decomposition with the boundary of group 19 projective representation .

sections.title: Retain lattice-translation remainders in Seitz multiplication
sections.text: The product of two selected representatives is not necessarily equal to the third representative in the catalog, and may be an additional full cell translation Δ. At fixed k this difference becomes a factor system and ordinary multiplication of quotient group cannot be imposed on the Bloch matrix.

sections.title: orthogonal inner product to multiplicity
sections.text: does the inner product with the verified little group irreducible character of the same factor system. The output must satisfy both the nonnegative integer multiplicity , the original character reconstruction, and the conservation of total dimensionality; simply listing some representation names is not enough to constitute a decomposition.

sections.title: Why are four s orbitals not equal to four one-dimensional representations?
sections.text: A general orbit of space group 19 has four sites. Screw phases at R=(1/2,1/2,1/2) give nontrivial projective multiplication, producing two copies of the same two-dimensional little-group irrep. This dimension comes from spatial operations and translation phases, rather than a Kramers conclusion imposed by spin time reversal.

sections.title: Local results and global problems
sections.text: Switching to point Γ, the factor system is trivial, and the s four-dimensional fiber is divided into four one-dimensional terms. D1 with different k is not the same global label. If you want to further connect energy bands, please enter the compatibility relationship class; this module does not automatically provide full-region connectivity diagrams or topological classifications.

lessons.title: The difference between perovskite sites and orbital centers
lessons.summary: Compares the induced space of the cubic origin, body-centered and three face-centered sites.

sections.title: Separate structural sites and electron filling
sections.text: The 1a, 1b and 3c positions of Pm−3m are site prototypes. The three face-center sites of 3c often illustrate the oxygen sublattice of ideal cubic perovskites, but this experiment places abstract local orbitals only, without charge transfer, covalent hybridization, actual oxygen levels or occupancies.

sections.title: p orbitals at the origin form a polar-vector triplet
sections.text: At Γ, local pₓ,pᵧ,p_z form the three-dimensional polar-vector representation of O_h, commonly labeled T_{1u}. Its inversion matrix is −I₃ and character −3. The program still supplies only verified local D labels, without identifying them as standard database labels.

sections.title: orbit center influence boundary character
sections.text: Local inversion is even for s orbitals at both the origin and body center. However, after inversion the body-center seed must be shifted by (−1,−1,−1) to return to the same  primitive cell  site, so parity changes sign at some boundary points. Orbital centers and the Bloch gauge must therefore be retained.
sections.formula: χ_I(k;r₀) = exp(+4πi k·r₀) (s orbital, inversion center)

sections.title: cross-module project
sections.text: Record the dimensions and inversion characters of 1a-s, 1b-s, and 3c-p at Γ, X, and R. Then discuss local orbitals in the crystal-field classroom and connectivity in the band-compatibility classroom. These address different levels of the same structural problem; these sampled data alone cannot determine whether the complete material is topological.

lessons.title: From diatomic equations of motion to two phonon branches
lessons.summary: Fix the mass normalization and Bloch gauge before examining energy and physical displacements.

sections.title: primitive cell  and two springs
sections.text: The A_l—B_l spring is K₁ and the B_l—A_{l+1} spring is K₂. The primitive-cell length is a and B lies at sa. K, masses and basis positions are independent inputs; changing s does not automatically refit the springs.

sections.title: Eigenvectors are not atomic displacements in a common unit
sections.text: The program solves a two-by-two  Hermitian  matrix in a mass-normalized basis. The Γ acoustic eigenvector is proportional to (√m_A,√m_B); divide by √m to obtain equal-amplitude, in-phase physical displacements of both atoms.

sections.title: Analytic checks of the two branch energies
sections.text: Define t=(K₁+K₂)(1/m_A+1/m_B) and d=4K₁K₂sin²(qa/2)/(m_A m_B). λ_{±} are dynamical-matrix eigenvalues, with energy conversion factor C≈64.654 meV. At Γ the lower branch is rigid translation and the upper branch is relative motion at finite frequency.

sections.title: Why the spectrum has no Γ-point zero-frequency peak
sections.text: The one-phonon formula contains 1/ε and cannot accept a rigid translation directly. The program retains zero-frequency dispersion but excludes modes below an explicit cutoff from the inelastic spectrum. Elastic and quasielastic peaks are not calculated; this does not artificially gap an acoustic mode.
sections.formula: ε<energyCutoff ⇒ exclude from the one-phonon spectrum

lessons.title: For the same  phonon , why does brightness differ between adjacent  reciprocal lattice  zones?
lessons.summary: Distinguish full Q from reduced q and combine projections, basis phases and mass factors in one amplitude.

sections.title: The scattering vector is not the reduced phonon momentum
sections.text: Q is the signed full scan coordinate; Q_{∥}=Qcosθ is its projection onto the chain axis. Reduced q folds into the first  Brillouin zone , while Q_{∥}−q is a  reciprocal lattice  vector. Two measurement points separated by a  reciprocal lattice  vector may have identical  phonon  energies but different intensities.

sections.title: Add amplitudes first, then square
sections.text: Coherent scattering requires adding the two atoms' complex amplitudes first. b is a signed relative scattering amplitude and e is a mass-normalized eigenvector. In the present gauge the creation amplitude must use the complex conjugate of e; omitting phases or conjugation changes extinctions.

sections.title: Calculate extinction by hand in the folded monatomic limit
sections.text: Set the two masses, two springs and two scattering amplitudes equal, with s=1/2. The chosen cell simply doubles a monatomic chain. The folded optical branch is extinct in even reciprocal zones, and the folded acoustic branch in odd zones. Switching the even/odd presets keeps the Hamiltonian fixed and changes only full Q.

sections.title: Treat directional projection and degeneracy separately
sections.text: When Q is perpendicular to the chain, the longitudinal Q·e vanishes and this entire model is dark. Changing the angle also changes reduced q, so cos²θ alone is insufficient. At exact degeneracy, individual-eigenvector intensities are not unique observables; the program reports the sum over the degenerate subspace.

lessons.title: Read temperature and model limits from Stokes / anti-Stokes signals
lessons.summary: Derive detailed balance from Bose factors, distinguishing broadening, cutoffs, material data, and actual lifetimes.

sections.title: Positive energy means the probe loses energy
sections.text: Here Stokes lies at +ε and creates a phonon, while anti-Stokes lies at −ε and annihilates an existing phonon. Their factors are n+1 and n, respectively. Phonons can therefore still be created at zero temperature, but no thermal phonon can be annihilated.

sections.title: Detailed balance tests individual-mode weights
sections.text: This model's real force constants and real scattering weights satisfy  time reversal , so creation and annihilation at the same Q have equal bare weights. The mode-by-mode ratio directly tests Bose statistics; if both processes are dark, their ratio has no experimental meaning.

sections.title: Broadening is not a lifetime, and sampling is not integration
sections.text: Gaussian σ is the standard deviation of the specified resolution; peak area preserves the weight. The program uses erf for finite-window integration and checks ΔE≤σ/2. Once tails cross zero energy or several peaks overlap, the intensity ratio at each sample no longer equals the simple detailed-balance formula.

sections.title: What must be added to move from this model to real files?
sections.text: Long-wavelength fluctuations of an infinite one-dimensional model and the omitted Debye–Waller factor cannot be ignored. This version does not accept real Phonopy scattering input: the existing importer retains complete eigenvectors only for the selected single mode. A realistic calculation needs the primitive cell, Å units, masses, complex eigenvectors for every mode, Q/q matching, scattering weights and suitable thermal-vibration factors. Report the low-energy cutoff and finite Q mesh with the results.

lessons.title: From equivalent domains to domain wall in space
lessons.summary: With the same two minimum values, why can the interface be neither infinitely steep nor infinitely wide?

sections.title: Add gradient cost to local free energy
sections.text: There have been phase transition experiments to find uniform minima. After letting φ change with the position, the local double well hopes to take ±v everywhere, and the gradient term hopes that the adjacent positions will be smooth; the two compete to determine the wall width.

sections.title: Fix the boundary and find the stationary point
sections.text: Fix the left endpoint at −v and the right at +v, then vary the interior φ. Boundary variations vanish; integration by parts gives a second-order equation. Choose the interface center at x=0.

sections.title: Continuous solution and width
sections.text: On the infinite domain, a tanh profile connects the two minima. Larger κ penalizes abrupt spatial changes and widens the wall; larger v or β strengthens the local restoring force.

sections.title: Teaching amount and material amount
sections.text: Here x, φ, and free energy are all in reduced units. BaTiO₃ only provides the background of 180° polar domain ; to calculate the material wall energy, real coefficients, electrostatic boundaries and elastic coupling are required.

lessons.title: Domain-wall energy and grid convergence
lessons.summary: Compare analytic tension, finite intervals, and discrete solutions, and understand the use of computational diagnostics.

sections.title: Wall energy is an additional price for a relatively homogeneous bulk phase
sections.text: Set the uniform ground state free energy at both ends to zero. The gradient term on the continuous equilibrium solution is equal to the local potential energy; integrating over the entire space yields the wall energy per area.

sections.title: Make a comparison that can be calculated by hand
sections.text: Fixed β=v=1 and changed κ from 1 to 4. Both width and wall energy are doubled. Wider walls do not necessarily mean cheaper, because what changes is the model parameters.

sections.title: The role of two grids
sections.text: program fixes the same finite interval and uses N and 2N-1 points to find discrete stationary points. The energy difference is an indication of the current discreteness sensitivity; a small stationary point residual does not mean that the continuous solution has converged.

sections.title: Stability and model boundaries
sections.text: The two boundary conditions force one wall to exist, while antisymmetry pins its center. This experiment finds a center-constrained static stationary point and also checks the Hessian after releasing that constraint. Coarse grids can create unstable directions, so a small residual alone does not establish stability. Domain nucleation, switching speeds and 3D domain morphology are not predicted.

lessons.title: SSH domain wall How to generate localized electronic states
lessons.summary: puts the inversion of bond order, finite chain energy spectrum and local density of states into the same research picture.

sections.title: Use bond order as another order parameter
sections.text: In the independent SSH model, alternating strong and weak bonds define dimerization order. Reverse it smoothly at the center and compare with uniform dimerization. Interface width uses bond spacings and is not equated numerically to a ferroelectric wall width.

sections.title: Pairing of Chiral Symmetry and Spectrum
sections.text: Without onsite potentials, the even/odd sublattice-sign operator anticommutes with the Hamiltonian, pairing energies ±E. Onsite potentials on the central two sites break this symmetry and change local spectra.

sections.title: Why look at energy and position at the same time?
sections.text: open chain can have terminal states and interface states at the same time, and the limited length will also cause hybridization. Observing the LDOS near E=0 and the center/boundary weights can distinguish the two. When the link is short or the interface is wide, the two areas may overlap. You need to check the area index and warning. Do not add the two weights.

sections.title: avoids the influence of arbitrary degenerate eigenvectors
sections.text: program treats all states of |E|<tδ as a subspace, and uses projection operator diagonal elements to display its density; the sum of densities is equal to the number of selected states. This quantity is unchanged within the selected subspace change of basis .

lessons.title: First select the particle number sector and then create a many-body base
lessons.summary: Build an occupation-number basis from the two spin states of a single spatial orbital, identifying fermionic signs and boundary conditions.

sections.title: One orbital per site, with four occupation possibilities
sections.text: Each site permits four local states: empty, ↑, ↓ and ↑↓. Identical spins cannot occupy the same orbital, while opposite spins may doubly occupy it at energy cost U. Single band here means one spatial orbital per site, not spinless electrons.

sections.title: Reduce the matrix using conserved quantities
sections.text: Hopping does not flip spin, so N_{↑} and N_{↓} are separately conserved. A fixed-sector dimension is the product of the site-choice counts for the two spins. The dimer (1,1) sector has four occupation-number basis states; the four-site (2,2) sector has 36, small enough to calculate every eigenvalue.

sections.title: Hopping operators must retain fermionic signs
sections.text: matrix elements are obtained by applying the creation and annihilation operators to the same fixed ordering occupancy number base. Crossing the occupied Fermi mode contributes a negative sign. Changing the basis ordering can change the sign of the matrix elements, but the eigenvalues ​​and physical expectation values ​​remain unchanged after the consistent transformation.
sections.formula: H=−t Σ_{⟨ij⟩,σ}(c_{iσ}†c_{jσ}+h.c.)+U Σ_i n_{i↑}n_{i↓}+Σ_i ε_i n_i

sections.title: Boundary conditions first change the bond list
sections.text: An open chain has L−1 nearest-neighbor bonds; a periodic chain adds the closing bond, counting each undirected pair once. This site’s two-site periodic model still has one bond, identical to open boundaries; the three-site ring is triangular. Check the bond list before spectra and do not double dimer hopping t.

lessons.title: How virtual hopping in a dimer produces antiferromagnetic exchange
lessons.summary: Use the exact singlet–triplet splitting to test the validity of 4t²/U.

sections.title: First compare the spin states that can take advantage of double occupation
sections.text: When two electrons occupy separate sites, hopping mixes a singlet with doubly occupied configurations and lowers its energy; the triplet is constrained by spin and fermionic antisymmetry. The symmetric dimer’s triplet energy is zero, while its lowest singlet lies below zero for t>0.

sections.title: Exact splitting with large U expansion
sections.text: This experiment compares the lowest S=0 and S=1 energies of the N=2 dimer. At Δ=0 an analytical expression exists. Only for U≫t does virtual double occupancy cost approximately U, giving 4t²/U. At U=0, the exact splitting is 2t and the large-U approximation is inapplicable.

sections.title: Double occupation did not disappear suddenly
sections.text: Scanning along U, the symmetric dimer double occupancy of finite t gradually decreases; it remains non-zero under finite positive U. Let D=Σ_i⟨n_{i↑}n_{i↓}⟩, then the half-filled dimer has D=∂E_S/∂U. Reducing D means that charge fluctuations are suppressed, which does not mean that a thermodynamic phase transition has been discovered.

sections.title: Spin correlation and exchange energy are not the same quantity
sections.text: ⟨S_1·S_2⟩ is a dimensionless correlation; J_ST is energy. In the dimer singlet state, the double occupied part does not carry local spin, so ⟨S_1·S_2⟩=−3(1−D)/4. When U/t increases, the correlation tends to −3/4, but the exchange energy scale tends to become smaller.

lessons.title: What kind of gaps are the gaps in the spectrum?
lessons.summary: differentiates between fixed S^z sector excitation, dimer S/T splitting and charge gain and loss energies that change electron number.

sections.title: Fixed sector spectrum only answers questions within the specified space
sections.text: The spectrum comes from the input (N_{↑},N_{↓}) sector, fixing both N and S^z. Its sector excitation gap compares the ground energy with the next level above the whole degenerate ground subspace. It need not be the lowest excitation across all spin sectors and is not automatically a charge gap. With only one distinct energy level, this gap is undefined.

sections.title: Charge addition/removal requires recalculating neighboring particle-number sectors
sections.text: For each total N, first take the lowest ground state energy E₀(N) among all allowed (N_{↑},N_{↓}), and then calculate the total energy cost of adding one electron and subtracting one electron. The high-energy spin sector selected by the user cannot be directly regarded as the total N ground state. The empty system N=0 and the full system N=2L lack the number of particles on one side, and the charge increase and decrease gap is not defined.

sections.title: U=0 Small systems can also have non-zero intervals
sections.text: symmetric dimer is half-filled, the charge increase and decrease gap is √(U²+16t²)−2t; U=0 is still equal to 2t because there are only discrete bonding and antibonding orbitals. This finite size gap is not an interaction-induced thermodynamic Mott gap. Changing L and the boundary will change the discrete spectrum.

sections.title: Four sites can test the mechanism, but cannot extrapolate the phase diagram
sections.text: Comparing the local density, double occupancy, and interbond correlation of four-site open chains and rings, one can see how boundaries affect the results. But two or four sites are not enough to determine long-range magnetic order, critical U, or the metal-to-insulator transition of real materials. The exact solution of the infinite one-dimensional uniform model is another problem, and this site does not implement Bethe Ansatz or thermodynamic limit extrapolation.

lessons.title: Potential energy difference, repulsion and degenerate average
lessons.summary: Observe charge shifts through inequivalent dimers and then use the atomic limit to examine the implications of ground state averaging.

sections.title: Positive Δ Which site should be raised?
sections.text: Internal indexing starts at i=0: the first site has onsite energy +Δ/2 and the second −Δ/2. Positive Δ favors moving electrons to the second site, while U opposes their simultaneous double occupancy there. Total-number conservation alone does not reveal this redistribution; compare site densities and double occupancy.

sections.title: Atomic limit gives clear energy competition
sections.text: dimers N=2 and t=0, the sum of the potential energies each occupying one site is 0; the energy of two electrons occupying the lower energy site is U−|Δ|. The two types of configurations meet in U=|Δ|. After the finite t is turned on and the configuration is mixed, the density change of the dimer usually appears as a smooth crossover and cannot be called a bulk material phase transition.

sections.title: At degeneracy, do not rely on an arbitrarily chosen eigenvector
sections.text: The program equally averages observables over degenerate ground states in the selected fixed sector, using tolerance 10⁻⁹ eV. Results do not depend on arbitrary numerical degenerate bases. This is not a finite-temperature calculation and does not mix S^z sectors automatically; different constraints may give different averages.

sections.title: Strict The difference between t=0 and t→0⁺
sections.text: In the dimer (1,1) sector of Δ=0 and U>0, t=0 has two separated degenerate ground states; the equal-weighted average yields ⟨S_1·S_2⟩=−1/4. Theoretically, non-zero t selects the lowest singlet state, and the correlation tends to −3/4 at t→0⁺; numerical calculations require S/T splitting greater than 10⁻⁹ eV to be resolved, and even minimal non-zero t may be degenerately averaged. Both limit orders and numerical tolerances must be noted.

exercises.title: Group 2: turn the site count into the fiber dimension
exercises.prompt: Choose the general-position two-site orbit and an s orbital, then work through the Γ-point derivation by hand.

steps.prompt: Is the inversion image of a general-position site r₀ equivalent to the site itself?
steps.hint: r₀=(0.17,0.23,0.31); check whether 2r₀ is an integer vector.
choices: Not equivalent; the orbit has two sites
Yes; the orbit contains only one point
steps.explanation: 2r₀ is not an integer vector, so r₀ and −r₀ are two sites within the primitive cell.

steps.prompt: What is the order of the seed site's stabilizer?
steps.hint: quotient group  has order 2; use the orbit– stabilizer  relation.

steps.prompt: What is the trace of the inversion matrix for the two s orbitals at Γ?
steps.hint: Inversion exchanges the two points, so the matrix diagonal receives no fixed-point contributions.
steps.explanation: The site-permutation matrix is off-diagonal: the inversion character is 0 and the identity character is 2.

steps.prompt: What are the multiplicities of the two one-dimensional parity representations?
steps.hint: Solve n_g+n_u=2, n_g−n_u=0.
choices: Zero even states, two odd states
steps.explanation: Adding and subtracting gives n_g=n_u=1; the dimensions also balance.

exercises.title: Group 4: derive ±i from two sites
exercises.prompt: Select the  screw axis  boundary preset and derive the result along the program's BC z axis.

steps.prompt: What spatial operation results from applying a 2₁ screw twice?
steps.hint: Two half-lattice translations combine into one full translation, and a twofold rotation squares to the identity.
choices: Translate half a lattice spacing along z
Translation by one lattice period along z
steps.explanation: S²={E|0,0,1}; squaring only the point operation instead of the complete space-group operation loses the translation.

steps.prompt: At k_z=1/2 in the periodic Bloch gauge, what is the phase of a full lattice translation?
steps.hint: Substitute into exp(−2πi k_z).
steps.explanation: exp(−πi)=−1, hence U_S²=−I.

steps.prompt: Which pair gives the spinless screw eigenvalues?
steps.hint: Solve λ²=−1.
steps.explanation: Two-site s orbitals provide the branches ±i;  time reversal  is not imposed here.

steps.prompt: Does the branch exchange of λ_{+} and λ_{−} in the figure give the band energy of the material?
steps.hint: There are no Hamiltonian parameters for this experiment.
choices: It has been proven that the insulating and topological
No; they are symmetry eigenvalues only
The conduction band and valence band have been given
steps.explanation: Symmetry representations constrain energy models but are not themselves energy dispersions or complete topological classifications.

exercises.title: Group 19: Two copies of the two-dimensional projective little group representation
exercises.prompt: Use the R-point s-orbital preset and check each basis for the decomposition.

steps.prompt: A general site orbit has four points, each carrying one s orbital. What is the fiber dimension?
steps.hint: The dimensionality is the number of sites multiplied by the number of local orbitals.
steps.explanation: m=4, d=1, so fiber dimension 4; no additional spin multiplication.

steps.prompt: Can point R ignore the extra integer vector when the representative elements are multiplied?
steps.hint: The component of k is 1/2, and some integer translations contribute a negative sign.
choices: No, it will change the factor system
Yes; full lattice translations always have phase 1
Only not available when there is SOC
steps.explanation: Bloch translation characters can be −1 at the boundary, quotient group needs to use the corresponding projective representation .

steps.prompt: The table of values ​​shows that only one 2D class irreducible representation contributes, what is its multiplicity ?
steps.hint: Use total dimensionality conservation 4=n×2.
steps.explanation: The two two-dimensional representations give exactly four-dimensional induced space; character inner product and reconstruction can be independently verified.

steps.prompt: Can this two-dimensionality be directly called spin Kramers degeneracy?
steps.hint: This module does not contain spin and time reversal .
choices: Yes, the two-dimensional must be equal to Kramers
No, what is verified here is the space little group projective algebra
steps.explanation: Kramers pairing requires an appropriate antiunitary symmetry squaring to −1; this experiment constructs only ordinary-space-group Bloch actions.

exercises.title: Place p orbitals on three face-centered sites
exercises.prompt: Start with the 3c-p prototype, then compare it with p orbitals at the origin.

steps.prompt: What is the orbit multiplicity m of 3c?
steps.hint: The site table contains three coordinate permutations.
steps.explanation: The three face-centered sites form one orbit with m=3.

steps.prompt: What is the fiber dimension given by the complete p triplet at each point?
steps.hint: 3 orbitals per point, but no spin.
steps.explanation: is 3×3=9; 18 requires additional spin, which is not available here.

steps.prompt: What is the character of the origin p triplet under inversion?
steps.hint: Every component of a polar vector changes sign.
steps.explanation: The inversion matrix is ​​−I₃, and the trace is −3. Don't think of it as axial vector .

steps.prompt: Has the full nine-dimensional 3c-p space been established as one EBR?
steps.hint: First determine whether the local representation is irreducible and check the complete EBR criterion.
choices: No, the program only verifies the decomposition of induced representation and little group
Yes; every site orbit is an EBR
Yes, as long as the dimensions are odd
steps.explanation: p is reducible in the 3c position stabilizer , and this module does not implement general elementary determination or full Brillouin zone topological analysis.

exercises.title: Derive mass factors from the translational zero mode
exercises.prompt: Use the diatomic-chain preset. Check Γ on paper before reading the computed result.

steps.prompt: What actual displacement corresponds to a rigid translation at Γ?
steps.hint: Translation changes no spring length.
choices: A and B move in phase with equal amplitudes
A and B move with equal amplitudes in opposite phases
The heavier atom must remain stationary
steps.explanation: Equal-amplitude in-phase motion preserves every relative distance and is therefore a zero-restoring-force  acoustic mode .

steps.prompt: What should the ratio of mass-normalized eigenvector components e_A:e_B be?
steps.hint: The physical displacement is e_{κ}/√m_{κ}.
steps.explanation: To obtain e_A/√m_A=e_B/√m_B, one needs e_A:e_B=√m_A:√m_B.

steps.prompt: At Γ, which quantity is proportional to the optical energy squared?
steps.hint: One eigenvalue of the two-by-two matrix is 0; the other equals its trace.
steps.explanation: λ_{op}=TrD=(K₁+K₂)(1/m_A+1/m_B), multiplied by the square of the energy-conversion constant.

steps.prompt: How should the Γ-point zero-frequency acoustic mode be handled in this inelastic spectrum?
steps.hint: The formula contains 1/ε; this page has no elastic-scattering model.
choices: Exclude it using the explicit low-energy cutoff and report it
Replace it with any finite energy
steps.explanation: Retain the zero-frequency dispersion but exclude it from the one-phonon inelastic formula; broadening or an arbitrary energy cannot be used to invent an elastic peak.

exercises.title: Extinctions interchange in adjacent reciprocal-lattice zones
exercises.prompt: Compare “identical atoms · even  reciprocal lattice  zone” with “adjacent odd  reciprocal lattice  zone”; only full Q changes.

steps.prompt: What happens to reduced q when Q increases by 2π/a?
steps.hint: Reduce modulo a reciprocal-lattice vector.
choices: Return to the same reduced q
steps.explanation: Reduced q is unchanged, so the same Hamiltonian has identical  phonon  energies.

steps.prompt: At s=1/2, what phase does the B basis atom acquire on crossing one reciprocal zone?
steps.hint: Evaluate exp[i(2π/a)(a/2)].
steps.explanation: The extra phase is exp(iπ)=−1. A is at the origin and gains no such phase.

steps.prompt: In an odd reciprocal zone, what are the acoustic and optical amplitude factors?
steps.hint: Substitute into 1+(−1)^n and 1−(−1)^n.
steps.explanation: Acoustic coherent amplitudes cancel while optical amplitudes add; this does not mean  acoustic mode  is absent.

steps.prompt: Why can the bare peak weights of the two presets not be compared using only 0 or 4?
steps.hint: The scattering formula also contains the full-Q projection, masses, and 1/energy.
choices: Retain Q∥², masses, and the 1/ε factor as well
Because the program changed the temperature
Because adjacent zones must have different force constants
steps.explanation: 0/4 is the interference factor. Different full-Q magnitudes also change Q∥², so bright-branch absolute relative weights need not agree.

exercises.title: Derive detailed balance from the energy-gain branch
exercises.prompt: Compare the zero-temperature and 300K presets at fixed model, Q, scattering amplitudes, cutoff, and broadening.

steps.prompt: For T=0, which unbroadened single-mode weights may be nonzero?
steps.hint: Substitute n=0 into W(n+1) and Wn.
steps.explanation: Stokes retains the +1 for zero-point creation; anti-Stokes requires an existing phonon, so its weight is zero.

steps.prompt: How does I_{−}/I_{+} simplify?
steps.hint: n/(n+1), with x=ε/kBT.
steps.explanation: n=1/(eˣ−1), hence n/(n+1)=e⁻ˣ.

steps.prompt: If ε=kBT, what is the approximate anti-Stokes/Stokes ratio?
steps.hint: Use e⁻¹.
steps.explanation: The ratio is about 0.3679, below 1; for a fixed energy the two weights become closer as temperature rises.

steps.prompt: Can increasing Gaussian broadening σ establish a shorter lifetime?
steps.hint: Here σ is the input energy resolution; no anharmonic self-energy has been calculated.
choices: It directly gives the actual lifetime
No; an independent decay model and resolution analysis are required
The energy integral must increase with σ
steps.explanation: A unit-area Gaussian changes peak width without changing its fully integrated weight. This page does not calculate phonon lifetimes.

exercises.title: Get the width of domain wall step by step

steps.prompt: Which penalizes spatial changes?
steps.hint: Observe whether it contains position derivatives.
steps.explanation: Gradient terms impose energy costs on rapid spatial changes.

steps.prompt: What is the stationary point equation given by fixed boundary variation?
steps.hint: The gradient term needs to be integrated by parts.
steps.explanation: δF/δφ=−κφ″+βφ(φ²−v²)=0。

steps.prompt: Substituting φ=v tanh(x/ξ), what is ξ?
steps.hint: Compare the coefficients multiplying tanh and sech².
steps.explanation: ξ²=2κ/(βv²), in this case ξ=√2.

steps.prompt: Only increases κ by 4 times, how does ξ change?
steps.hint: ξ is proportional to √κ.
steps.explanation: The gradient cost becomes larger and the equilibrium wall width increases by 2 times.

exercises.title: Wall energy and numerical reliability
exercises.prompt: Check the baseline model and κ=4 model.

steps.prompt: What is the benchmark infinite continuous wall energy?
steps.hint: into σ=2√(2κβ)v³/3.

steps.prompt: κ=4 What is the wall energy when β and v are constant?
steps.hint: Wall energy is also proportional to √κ.
steps.explanation: Both wall width and wall energy are increased by 2 times.

steps.prompt: The stationary point residual error is very small, but the grid energy difference is obvious. What should be done?
steps.hint: Discrete equations and continuous limits are two different tests.
choices: is directly called the precise material wall energy
Add grid and compare the same intervals
steps.explanation: The discrete error needs to be checked and the limited interval extended if necessary.

steps.prompt: Can the current energy be quoted directly as a BaTiO₃ wall energy in J/m²?
steps.hint: No true length/polarization/energy scales are given here.
choices: As long as the curve is smooth
No, material coefficient and unit scale are required
steps.explanation: The reduced teaching model only describes the mechanism and parameter scaling.

exercises.title: Distinguish between interface state and terminal state
exercises.prompt: Compare the wall-ssh, uniform-chain and central-onsite-potential presets.

steps.prompt: Which quantity changes sign across space in the SSH experiment?
steps.hint: Observe adjacent strong and weak bonds.
steps.explanation: A sign reversal of alternating hopping connects two bond-order patterns.

steps.prompt: Which relationship holds when there is no potential?
steps.hint: Γ has opposite signs on the two sublattices.
steps.explanation: Chiral symmetry leads to ±E energy spectrum pairing, and finite chains can still have hybrid splitting.

steps.prompt: After discovering the near-zero energy level, how to confirm that it is at the interface?
steps.hint: Energy cannot provide spatial location.
choices: Only look at the absolute value of energy
Look at the LDOS/projection weights of the center and borders simultaneously
steps.explanation: Open chains may also have terminal states, requiring position-resolved evidence.

steps.prompt: When two nearly degenerate states are replaced by a set of orthogonal basis, which quantity remains unchanged?
steps.hint: Sums the entire selected subspace.
choices: Each component of an arbitrary eigenvector
steps.explanation: is unchanged for the unitary change of basis inside the selected subspace.

exercises.title: From half-filled to 36-dimensional matrix
exercises.prompt: Use the four-site half-filled preset; first calculate basis size by hand, then check boundary conditions.

steps.prompt: L=4 and N_{↑}=N_{↓}=2, what is the total number of electrons and S^z?
steps.hint: add and subtract respectively.
steps.explanation: N=2+2=4, an average of one electron per site; S^z=(2−2)/2=0.

steps.prompt: What is the dimension of the fixed (2,2) sector?
steps.hint: Two spins choose 2 from 4 sites respectively.
steps.explanation: C(4,2)²=6²=36; 256 is the full Fock space dimension without any fixed number of particles.

steps.prompt: How will the number of undirected bonds change after the four-site open chain is changed to a periodic chain?
steps.hint: Add only the bond joining the first and last sites.
steps.explanation: An open chain has bonds 01,12,23; periodic boundaries add 30. Both hopping directions per bond are already included via h.c.

steps.prompt: Should hopping t be doubled in this site’s two-site periodic model?
steps.hint: Count each undirected bond only once.
choices: No, the two-site opening boundary is the same as the period boundary.
Yes; periodic boundaries must give two independent bonds
steps.explanation: Closing a two-site chain still joins the same site pair; adding that bond twice changes the defined model.

exercises.title: Testing superexchange with dimer exact solution
exercises.prompt: takes t=1 eV, U=4 eV, Δ=0, and N=2 to compare the exact energy and approximation.

steps.prompt: Which is the lowest singlet energy E_S?
steps.hint: calculates (4−√32)/2.
steps.explanation: Hopping mixes doubly occupied configurations into the singlet, lowering its energy to about −0.828427 eV.

steps.prompt: The triplet energy is 0, what is the exact S/T splitting?
steps.hint: J_ST=E_T−E_S。
steps.explanation: splits to about 0.828427 eV; it is positive energy, not negative spin correlation.

steps.prompt: 4t²/U Given 1 eV here, how should we judge?
steps.hint: U/t=4 is not infinite.
choices: It is a large U approximation, here it is higher than the exact value
It must be exactly the same as the exact value
The exact solution should be replaced with this value
steps.explanation: Higher-order terms still contribute at finite U/t; you should scan along U to observe how the relative error decreases.

steps.prompt: As U continues to increase, which set of trends applies to this symmetric dimer?
steps.hint: Compare the analytical expression of D with J_ST≈4t²/U.
choices: double occupancy is reduced, J_ST is reduced
double occupancy remains unchanged, J_ST increases
steps.explanation: Charge fluctuations and exchange energy both decrease while spin correlation approaches −3/4. Stronger antiferromagnetic correlations do not imply larger exchange energy.

exercises.title: Don’t confuse the three energy gaps
exercises.prompt: First consider the half-filled dimer of U=0, and then examine the particle number boundary.

steps.prompt: Which set of energy is used for the charge increase and decrease gap?
steps.hint: The total number of particles needs to be changed.
choices: The difference between any two fixed S^z energy levels
The difference between two spin states of the same N
steps.explanation: Each of E₀ must take the minimum value among all allowed spin sectors of the total N.

steps.prompt: For a half-filled dimer with t=1,U=Δ=0, what is the charge-addition/removal gap?
steps.hint: uses √(U²+16t²)−2t.
steps.explanation: √16−2=2 eV, which is a finite size interval caused by discrete single particle energy levels.

steps.prompt: Does this nonzero gap at U=0 establish a Mott-insulating phase?
steps.hint: In this example there is no inter-electron repulsion and no thermodynamic limit is taken.
choices: Yes, any non-zero gap is called Mott gap
No, it is necessary to distinguish between finite size and interaction effects
Yes, just change to period boundary
steps.explanation: The spectrum of finite clusters is inherently discrete; the phase of an infinite system cannot be determined solely by the energy gap of two sites.

steps.prompt: How should the charge addition/removal gap be reported at N=0?
steps.hint: N−1 has no physical particle number sector.
choices: is forced to be recorded as 0
is not defined and indicates that the number of particles on one side is missing.
steps.explanation: Empty or full systems cannot perform bilateral additions and subtractions; missing values cannot be disguised as zero energy gaps.

exercises.title: Potential energy competition and atomic limit averaging
exercises.prompt: First take the dimers t=0, U=4, and Δ=6 eV, and then set Δ to 0.

steps.prompt: For positive Δ=6, what are the two sites’ onsite energies?
steps.hint: The first site corresponds to the internal index i=0.
steps.explanation: ε₀=+Δ/2, ε₁=−Δ/2, the second site is lower.

steps.prompt: N=2 and t=0, what is the energy of both electrons at the low energy site?
steps.hint: U plus twice the low site potential.
steps.explanation: U−|Δ|=4−6=−2 eV, below 0 eV of one electron per site.

steps.prompt: Set Δ=0 while keeping t=0 and U>0. How should the (1,1)-sector ground states be treated?
steps.hint: Two separate configurations are degenerate.
choices: Choose any one and treat the choice as the only physical state
Equally weighted average of the ground state subspace of the selected sector
steps.explanation: equal-weighted averaging does not rely on degenerate eigenvectors returned by diagonalization; the program does not automatically include other S^z sectors.

steps.prompt: Which ⟨S_1·S_2⟩ is given by this strict t=0 fixed S^z equal weight average?
steps.hint: Both separated product states have S^z_1 S^z_2=−1/4; the equal mixture has zero transverse average.
steps.explanation: −3/4 corresponds to the pure singlet state and is also the limit of t→0⁺; the degenerate average of strict t=0 is different from this limit.

cases.title: Orbital center and boundary parity
cases.summary: Compare the inversion character of the origin s and the body center s at point X for the same local dual symmetry.
cases.assumption: Abstract spin-free local orbit; fixed period specification and the same origin, topological conclusions cannot be directly given from two sampling points.

cases.title: Along-axis tangent in three-dimensional spiral crystal
cases.summary: tracks the spiral eigenphase on the z-tangential line of SG4/19, connecting the real-space half-lattice displacement and the momentum space factor system.
cases.assumption: This is an instructional model of the three-dimensional space group acting on a k-line, with no actual materials or hopping Hamiltonian specified.

cases.title: Site skeleton of ideal cubic perovskite
cases.summary: Use 1a/1b/3c of Pm−3m to understand the different sublattices and calculate a nine-dimensional representation of p orbitals at three face-centered sites.
cases.assumption: Only borrows the perovskite-type site skeleton; does not predict the true electronic bands, filling, phonon , or phase transitions of SrTiO₃ or BaTiO₃.

cases.title: Boundary of group 19 representation dimension
cases.summary: Compare the local representations of Γ and R, and then use the existing compatibility relationship to discuss in class why cross-k tracking cannot only recognize the D number.
cases.assumption: No inverse unitary symmetry is attached; the two-dimensionality of space projective representation and the spin Kramers mechanism must be distinguished.

cases.title: A mass-contrast prototype for a binary ionic lattice
cases.kind: An ideal model with material context
cases.summary: Use the A/B mass difference to understand acoustic and optical branches, then compare bare weights with visible spectral intensity.
cases.assumption: Only the mass contrast of binary ions is borrowed. The one-dimensional springs and relative b values are teaching parameters, not fits to NaCl's three-dimensional dispersion, polarization, long-range Coulomb interactions, or measured spectrum.

cases.title: The same vibrational mode becomes dark in a different measurement zone
cases.summary: Keep the model and reduced q fixed while changing only the reciprocal zone. Connect basis interference to diffraction extinction, while recognizing that the two use different structure factors.
cases.assumption: The monatomic folded limit, equal b values, and s=1/2 ensure analytic extinction. Inelastic amplitudes also contain eigenvectors, masses, and Q projections, so elastic diffraction intensities cannot simply be copied.

cases.title: From inspecting Phonopy files toward measurable phonon intensities
cases.summary: First check the structure, masses and selected mode in the existing tools, then list the full inputs required for one-phonon intensity. Use the thermal-occupation model to understand an experimental energy-gain branch.
cases.assumption: This version's scattering calculation runs only the diatomic model and does not accept Phonopy files. Frequencies, DOS, or a single-mode animation cannot reconstruct all-mode eigenvectors; the teaching heatmap must not be presented as an imported material's result.

cases.title: BaTiO₃ Background: From polar domain to scalar wall
cases.summary: From the existing polarity distortion and six-directional domains, select two opposite domains to build a one-dimensional continuous wall.
cases.assumption: Scalar 180° teaching wall; does not include material fitting, elastic and electrostatic boundaries.
links: Uniform phase transition and directional domain

cases.title: Dimerization chain: interface and terminal states appear simultaneously
cases.summary: Differentiates interface and boundary contributions using finite chain energy spectroscopy, LDOS and projected density.
cases.assumption: is a spin-free, non-interaction one-dimensional model, not a polyacetylene material parameter fitting.

cases.title: How does local potential change the interface spectrum?
cases.summary: fixed the transition and length, added potential only at the two central grid points, and compared the chiral residual and LDOS.
cases.assumption: local in-potential destroys chiral symmetry; the threshold filtering of near-zero energy subspace will change with the movement of energy levels.

cases.title: Minimum transition-exclusion model of molecular dimers
cases.summary: Use a two-site model to understand electron delocalization, double-occupancy penalty, and singlet stabilization between two local orbitals.
cases.assumption: These are two abstract orbitals inspired by molecular dimers and are not a quantitative model of an organic salt; they do not include molecular structure, lattice network, long-range Coulomb interactions, or fitted material parameters.

cases.title: From local electron repulsion to short range antiferromagnetic correlation
cases.summary: Observation of double-occupancy suppression and short-range spin correlation on a four-site half-filled chain and comparison of open boundaries to rings.
cases.assumption: only borrows the single-orbit effective model motivation from the discussion of copper-oxide systems; the four-site chain on this site does not have an explicit oxygen p orbital, two-dimensional CuO₂ structure or charge transfer energy, and does not predict the magnetic order, superconductivity or Mott transition of copper-oxide materials.

cases.title: Charge redistribution between unequal sites
cases.summary: Change Δ and U, compare the electron preference for low potential energy sites and the competition to avoid double occupancy, and use density instead of only energy to judge the change.
cases.assumption: The staggered potential energy is an additional single-orbital model parameter; it is not equal to the real ligand-to-metal charge transfer energy, and there is no self-consistent shielding, structural relaxation, or material parameter fitting.

cases.title: Degeneracy checking in strict atomic limits
cases.summary: Set t to 0, check for zero double occupancy, ground state degeneracy and fixed S^z equal weighted average, and compare with a very small non-zero t.
cases.assumption: The zero-temperature degenerate ground state is equally weighted by the selected particle number sector; this is not a temperature scan, nor does it represent a spontaneously selected magnetic state. Finite clusters alone cannot determine thermodynamically long programs.
